rows.unit: Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-10) total divided by 40

source.title: Cohen & Janicki-Deverts (2012), Who's stressed? Distributions of psychological stress in the United States in probability samples from 1983, 2006, and 2009. J Applied Social Psychology 42(6):1320-1334

rows.note: Weighted U.S. adult means from Table 1: 1983 13.0 (0.33 of 40), 2006 15.3 (0.38), 2009 15.8 (0.40); SD about 7.5 (0.19). By group (2009 PSS): under 25 16.8; 65+ 11.1; unemployed 16.6; retired 12.3; income $25k or less 17.8, $75k+ 14.7; women 16.1, men 15.5. Use these as checks and cohort spreads, never as draws. 0.25 is below every sample. Only valid if the game's normalized stress channel is defined as PSS-10/40; if it is a different construct the mapping is a modeling choice. No post-2009 probability-sample PSS-10 norm was found (not searched beyond this paper).
rows.whatItFakes: Prototype opening baseline on a normalized stress channel. No claim of a US population norm.

rows.unit: net affect (PANAS positive minus negative) divided by 40, on a -1 to +1 channel

source.title: PANAS state norms, Heubeck & Wilkinson (2019), non-clinical Australian adults 18-50, n=1,059, as listed by NovoPsych (secondary page)
source.table_or_section: Normative data section (PA 26.48, SD 8.1; NA 14.80, SD 5.49)

rows.note: Net = 26.48 - 14.80 = +11.68 on a -40..+40 range = +0.29. A U.S./UK primary norm would be better: Crawford & Henry (2004, Br J Clin Psychol 43:245-265, UK n=1,003) is the standard norms paper, but the publisher page returned 403 and I did not verify its values; Watson, Clark & Tellegen (1988) norms also not verified. The time instruction of the Australian norms was not stated on the page. Design caution: if the channel is a deviation from each person's own set point, 0 is legitimate and the population norm only informs between-person spread. As a population level, 'neutral 0' sits below the observed positive balance.
rows.whatItFakes: Neutral signed prototype affect channel before any recorded event. PANAS uses separate positive and negative channels, so this is an approximation.

source.title: P0-5 Mood, stress and choice (existing repo research); plus Lucke et al. 2025 and Verduyn & Lavrijsen 2015 added
source.table_or_section: P0-5 rows and 'gaps' entry; Lucke et al. Table 2; Verduyn & Lavrijsen Fig. 1

rows.note: Repo P0-5 (Wang et al. 2020, 859 employed U.S. adults): 28-minute affect autocorrelation .27-.41 across seven emotions, equal to AR(1) half-lives of about 15-22 minutes; the file says day-scale constants (this 2-day mood half-life and the 7-day stress half-life) cannot be identified from it and should stay registered tunables. New bounds: Lucke et al. 2025 (Cognition & Emotion 40(6); 254 adults, 5 prompts a day for up to 42 days): within-day autoregression NA .28 / PA .36, overnight .19 / .19, so most of an ordinary deviation is gone by the next morning. Verduyn & Lavrijsen 2015 (Motivation & Emotion 39:119-127; 233 students recalling episodes): median emotion lasts about 2 h to first return to baseline and 5 h to permanent return; sadness is longest (about 120 h per press summary of the paper's Fig. 1); long episodes track event importance and rumination. So 2 days is long for ordinary events and short for grief or very important events. Recommend scaling the half-life by event importance and brooding (0.2 day ordinary to about 5 days high-importance, months for bereavement per repo P0-8) instead of one scalar; if one scalar must stay, about 1 day. These AR figures include measurement noise; they bound, they do not identify.
rows.whatItFakes: Smooth analytic decay spanning hours to days; prototype estimate pending empirical decay calibration.

source.title: P0-5 Mood, stress and choice (existing repo research); plus Lee 2012 review of PSS test-retest
source.table_or_section: P0-5 gaps entry; Lee (2012) Asian Nursing Research 6:121-127, reliability section

rows.note: Keep 7 days as an in-range tunable. Bounds: PSS-10 scores correlate above .70 across retests 2 days to 4 weeks apart and r = .55 at 6 weeks (Lee 2012, reviewing Cohen, Kamarck & Mermelstein 1983), i.e. weeks of persistence; converted to an AR-equivalent that is about 49-54 days, but that includes stable between-person differences, so it is a ceiling for event-born stress, not a decay rate. Lower bound: ordinary mood carry-over is gone overnight (.19, Lucke et al. 2025). Persistent stressors (job loss, caregiving, illness) should be modeled as ongoing sources, not as slow decay (repo P0-5 says the same). Repo P0-5 also concludes no day-scale stress constant is identifiable from the sources it extracted.
rows.whatItFakes: Persistent stress can outlast transient affect; prototype estimate pending empirical decay calibration.

source.table_or_section: SCF Table 6 sheet '6 19 %s & medians' rows for median holdings; CE Table 1101 'Average annual expenditures' mean row

rows.note: 30 days happens to equal the all-family central value (SCF 2019 median $5,300 / CE mean spending $63,036 per year = 30.7 days), so it is defensible as a single default but hides a tenfold spread by income. Medians by income percentile (2019 dollars): <20 $810, 20-39.9 $2,050, 40-59.9 $4,315, 60-79.9 $10,000, 80-89.9 $20,000, 90-100 $70,000; CE spending by quintile $28,672 / $40,472 / $53,045 / $71,173 / $121,571. Caveats: my division, not a published statistic; mean spending in the denominator exceeds median spending (true median days would be somewhat longer); transaction accounts exclude cash on hand, other savings and credit lines; 5.7% of the lowest-income families hold no transaction account at all (SCF 2019: 94.3% hold one), and the medians are for holders only; SCF families and CE consumer units are not identical units; the top quintile spans two SCF groups. Repo main already holds the SCF 2022 income-percentile medians (900 / 2,550 / 7,400 / 15,760 / 33,800 / 111,600, 2022 dollars) but not paired with a spending base. Repo P0-4 notes currency in hand has no source. Recommend the income-percentile table in place of one constant.

source.title: Drive doc 00s PACKAGES (P8 CORE defect 3, cites Hall 2019 and Roberts & Dunbar 2015); Hall (2018/2019) How many hours does it take to make a friend? J Social and Personal Relationships 36(4):1278-1296, thresholds checked via KU news release

rows.note: Derived, not published: if 200 hours together is full closeness, one 1.92-hour contact (socialHours, ATUS 2025) adds 0.0096; if 50 hours is full, 0.038. The current 0.05 saturates in about 38 hours (20 contacts), roughly five times faster than the close-friend threshold. Caveats: Hall's samples were recent movers and college freshmen; social time counted, work time counted for little; people who stayed acquaintances had spent 30 h or less; kin closeness is not hours-based. Drive 00s also names Roberts & Dunbar 2015 half-lives of 18 and 36 months for fading (not re-verified). Owner ruling 2026-09-22: no universal rate and no 'friendship plus one' number, so treat this as a plausibility bound for the P9 check.

Name-recognition persistence: Bahrick et al. 1975 (J Exp Psychol: General 104:54-75; 392 graduates tested 2 weeks to 57 years after graduation) found classmate name recognition stays high for decades; secondary summaries say about 90% within 15 years and about 80% near 48 years but disagree, and I did not verify them from the paper. 2017-18 NTPS values (about 21 primary, 17 middle, 16 high self-contained) came from a secondary summary and were not verified. Drive doc 00s asks that every resident get such a circle from the same rule and shared dated events.

recommended.rule_when_budgets_land: impulse = change in real public purchases (and transfers/taxes) as a share of output x a multiplier; use purchases multiplier about 1.2 at one year, 1.5 at two years, below 1 for own-financed state/local spending; do not apply one multiplier to transfers and taxes (no matched US estimate found).

source.title: Research handoff: realized public money and local macro magnitudes (2026-09-22)
source.table_or_section: Closest US empirical evidence table; Requested channels: evidence status

rows.note: Zero is the right neutral average (trend growth already carries average public spending). Real bounds: Monacelli-Perotti-Trigari 2010 (spending +1% GDP -> output multiplier about 1.2 at one year, 1.5 at two; unemployment -0.6 point at peak); Chodorow-Reich 2019 cross-section 1.8; Nakamura-Steinsson 2014 about 1.5 (relative state output); Clemens-Miran 2012 below 1 for own-financed state spending; county panel: federal 1.5, state/local below 1. Direct measure of the impulse: Brookings Hutchins Fiscal Impact Measure, quarterly contribution to real GDP growth, e.g. Q3 2025 +0.3 (Jan 2026 estimate), Q4 2025 -1.2 (six-week shutdown), Q2 2026 -0.1 (published Sep 30 2026). Transfers, taxes collected and monthly decay for state/local own-source dollars: UNKNOWN in the literature. The replacement (M1-07 budgets read as monthly indexed totals) is a mechanic; research only bounds its size.
rows.whatItFakes: Public budgets add no impulse to national output beyond their real average.
